prime.problem: You now know how to fix one hidden layer by hand. A 50-layer net would need 50 hand-tuned scales and 50 wasted biases, and PyTorch's ready-made layers quietly use defaults that differ from the ones you picked.
prime.fits: This card takes the BatchNorm layer from the previous two cards and shows where it sits in a real architecture (ResNet-50), then maps your hand-written MLP pieces onto PyTorch's nn.Linear and nn.BatchNorm1d. The next card rebuilds those modules yourself.
prime.goal: Read a real model file and spot the repeated motif, explain why its convs have no bias, and know which PyTorch defaults to override for your own nets.

attend: Why does ResNet's conv layer carry no bias while its BatchNorm layer does have a β?
What is the same between a convolution and nn.Linear, so that the same motif applies to images?
How far is nn.Linear's default init from the Kaiming-tanh scale, and why does that gap stop mattering once BN follows it?
Which nn.BatchNorm1d default would hurt the lecture's batch-32 MLP, and through which buffer does the harm show up?
Why do the lecture's BN class and PyTorch's disagree in training output but agree in running_var?

must: BN subtracts each column's batch mean → any constant added before it cancels → the bias gets zero gradient → real nets set bias=False and let BN's β be the bias

Weight layer → BN → nonlinearity → every nonlinearity sees preactivations of a controlled scale regardless of the weight init → one unit can be stacked 50 deep without per-layer gain tuning (ResNet-50 = 16 Bottlenecks × 3 motifs + 2)

PyTorch BN momentum defaults to 0.1 → each batch-32 mean gets 10% weight in the running estimate → the buffer tracks batch noise (0.0570 vs 0.0076 with 0.001) → set a smaller momentum for small batches
Lecture BN normalises with x.var() (divide by n − 1), PyTorch with divide by n → training outputs differ by up to √(32/31) = 1.016 → both store the n − 1 version in running_var, so eval mode agrees
elevated: nn.Linear's default init is uniform in ±1/√fan_in → std 1/√(3·fan_in) = 0.1054 for fan_in 30, about 2.9× smaller than Kaiming-tanh → it matters in a net with no norm layer, much less when BN follows
reference: the full nn.BatchNorm1d signature: eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, track_running_stats=True, plus torch 2.14's keyword-only bias
BN buffer names: running_mean, running_var, num_batches_tracked; γ and β are .weight and .bias

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one ResNet Bottleneck block as boxes and arrows and annotate where the bias is missing and why. Then in 2–3 sentences say which two PyTorch defaults differ from what you did by hand in this lecture.
checklist: three rows of weight (conv) → BatchNorm → ReLU, with the last ReLU after the skip addition
bias=False on every conv because BN's mean subtraction cancels a bias; β takes over
a conv is the same W·x as Linear, applied to image patches
BN momentum 0.1 by default vs the lecture's 0.001 for batch 32

retrieve.q: Explain why adding a Linear bias right before BatchNorm is pure waste, in terms of what BN computes on each column.
answer: BN subtracts the column's batch mean
a bias shifts every example in that column by the same amount, so it shifts the mean by exactly that amount and cancels
so its gradient is 0 (4.4e-10 in the batchnorm-forward lab) and β provides the shift instead

retrieve.q: Walk one input x through a torchvision Bottleneck.forward: list each operation in order and say where the saved input comes back in.
answer: conv1 (1×1) → bn1 → relu
conv2 (3×3) → bn2 → relu
conv3 (1×1) → bn3
add the identity (or its downsampled version) → relu

retrieve.q: You swap the lecture's hand-written layers for nn.Linear and nn.BatchNorm1d with all defaults, batch 32. Which defaults would you override, and what would you see if you didn't?
answer: bias=False on the Linear before BN, or 200 dead parameters per layer
momentum lower than 0.1, or the running stats jitter with each batch and eval-mode loss suffers
init is fine to leave under BN, but not in a net with no norm layer (std 0.1054 vs 0.3043)

retrieve.q: Count the weight layers in ResNet-50 from its block structure, and say what the count tells you about why hand-tuned gains would not scale.
answer: [3, 4, 6, 3] = 16 Bottlenecks × 3 convs = 48
+ stem conv + final Linear = 50
50 scales to balance by hand; errors compound with depth, which BN removes

compare.q: This card uses PyTorch's modules; that card rebuilds them. What does rebuilding reveal that reading the signature hides, and where does your rebuilt BN differ from nn.BatchNorm1d?
answer: rebuilding shows __call__, .parameters(), the .training flag and buffers as plain code
the signature only shows defaults, not the variance formula
the lecture's class normalises with the n − 1 variance, PyTorch with n (max diff 0.0588 on a batch of 32)
both default to momentum 0.1 in that chapter

compare.q: GPT keeps a weight → norm → nonlinearity rhythm but uses LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm. Which design choice differs, and when does BN's choice fail where LayerNorm's doesn't?
answer: BN normalises each feature across the batch; LayerNorm normalises each example across its features
BN couples examples, needs running stats for eval, and has no variance for a batch of 1
LayerNorm behaves the same in training and inference and doesn't care about batch size
pick BN for big-batch vision nets; LayerNorm for sequence models and small or variable batches

predict.q: After training, you want to delete a BatchNorm layer at inference by folding it into the Linear before it (the lecture's exercise E02). With bias=False on that Linear, what new parameter must the folded Linear gain, and why?
predict.answer: A bias. At eval time BN is a fixed affine map per column: γ·(z − running_mean)/√(running_var + eps) + β. Folding multiplies each weight column by γ/√(running_var + eps) and needs a new bias β − γ·running_mean/√(running_var + eps). The bias you removed for training comes back once the batch statistics are frozen.

apply.task: Write the Build-it block again with nn.Linear(30, 200) (bias on) and torch.manual_seed(2147483647). Run one forward and backward pass on x = torch.randn(32, 30) with loss = (block(x)**2).mean(), then print the largest absolute value of the Linear's bias.grad and of its weight.grad.
apply.done: The parameter count reads 6600; the bias gradient is at float-rounding size (4.1e-10 on the M3) while the weight gradient is not (2.9e-3).
apply.hint: The batchnorm-forward lab measured the same effect on the lecture MLP: b1.grad max |.| was 4.4e-10.
